newsitem.title: NIGERIA: Nigeria industry wants steps to jump-start economy.
newsitem.headline: Nigeria industry wants steps to jump-start economy.

text.p: The umbrella organisation of Nigerian businesses called on the military government on Thursday to take measures in next year's fiscal budget to revive the economy.

"Steps need to be taken in the 1997 fiscal year to accelerate recovery and stimulate growth by cautiously reflating the economy while putting inflation under check," the Nigerian Association of Chambers of Commmerce, Industry, Mines and Agriculture (NACCIMA) said in a pre-budget memorandum sent to the government.

The group said economic recession had persisted with the purchasing power of Nigerians declining, unemployment and poverty levels increasing while manufacturing capacity utilisation stood at just 31 per cent.

"Bold measures need to be introduced to jump-start the economy in 1997 and send a clear message of the government's intention to allow market principles to hold sway in the allocation of resources," NACCIMA said.
Nigeria's economy, the largest in Sub-Saharan Africa, has been stagnant since 1993 when the army annulled an election that were due to restore democracy.

Over the last 18 months, the General Sani Abacha government, which took power in the mayhem precipitated by the annulment, has implemented free market policies that have succeeded in bringing about broad macro-economic stability.
But this is yet to translate into the economic growth the populous African country needs to make a difference in ordinary peoples' lives.
NACCIMA said the government should maintain the measures in place and even go further in its deregulation of the economy.
It said the government should merge the official and autonomous foreign exchange rates in 1997.

The government currently maintains an official exchange rate of 22 naira to the U.S. dollar for a few government transactions while all other foreign exchange business is done on the autonomous market rate currently about 80 naira to the dollar.
NACCIMA said "The dual exchange rate has continued to raise issues bordering on transparency and efficiency in allocation and use of foreign exchange resources in the public sector."
It also said the government should base its revenue expectations next year on crude oil price averaging $16 per barrel, the same as for this year's budget.
Nigeria depends on oil exports for more than 90 percent of its foreign exchange income.

NACCIMA urged the government to restrict tax payable by manufacturers to company tax only and to privatise the oil industry as well as the electricity and telecommunications sector as has been stated by cabinet ministers.
It said the military government should also keep to its promise to hand over power to elected civilians in 1998.
"In any economy, investment is a key function of the political environment. In the light of this, the current transition programme should be faithfully implemented," it said.
